LESSONS.title: Deriving the Laws of Indices — Part 2: Power, Negative, and Fractional Indices

slo.purpose: To extend learners' understanding of index notation by deriving the power rule, negative index rule, and fractional index rule, and connecting these to real-life contexts including the Kericho tea farm phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: By the end of this lesson, learners should be able to: (a) derive and apply the power rule of indices — (a^m)^n = a^(mn); (b) derive and apply the negative index rule — a^(−n) = 1/a^n; (c) derive and apply the fractional index rule — a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a and a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(a^m); (d) connect fractional indices to roots in context.
slo.skills: Deriving mathematical rules from first principles using pattern recognition; applying laws of indices accurately in simplification and computation; interpreting index expressions set in real-life Kenyan contexts; updating a Driving Question Board with new evidence.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the elegance and efficiency of mathematical notation; show curiosity about why fractional exponents correspond to roots; demonstrate persistence when deriving rules from first principles; value collaborative reasoning.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply indices in real-life situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1 and 2 learners established the product rule (a^m × a^n = a^(m+n)) and quotient rule (a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n)) using the Kericho tea farm's harvest data expressed as powers of 2. This lesson advances the storyline by asking: what happens when a power is itself raised to a power (scaling the estate), what does 2^0 or 2^(−1) mean in terms of harvest, and — most provocatively — what does 2^(1/2) mean for a 'half harvest cycle'? These three new rules complete the full set of index laws and set the stage for Lesson 4, where logarithms are introduced as the inverse operation that makes multiplying powers as easy as adding their exponents.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials are used in this lesson. Learners work with pencil-and-paper derivations and manipulatives. Ensure adequate desk space for group work. If printed 'harvest cards' are used, handle paper cutting with care.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting what (2^3)^2 and 2^(1/2) might mean in terms of the Kericho tea farm harvest, drawing on their existing understanding of repeated multiplication. Through a structured derivation activity (Observe phase), groups use the quotient rule established in Lesson 2 to prove the power rule, negative index rule, and fractional index rule from first principles — using powers of 2 as a consistent anchor. In the Explain phase, learners apply all three rules to simplify expressions and solve contextualised problems (scaling farm plots, interpreting sub-harvest cycles, reversing compound growth). A whole-class DQB update captures what has been resolved and what new questions have emerged. The lesson closes with learners revising their cumulative index-laws model to incorporate the three new rules, annotating each with a Kericho farm interpretation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are presented with three index expressions on the board — (2^3)^2, 2^0, and 2^(1/2) — each labelled with a farm scenario: (i) 'The farm manager squares the number of harvest cycles'; (ii) 'A plant completes zero harvest cycles'; (iii) 'A plant completes exactly half a harvest cycle.' Working individually for 3 minutes, learners write their numeric predictions and a one-sentence justification in their exercise books using only what they already know about repeated multiplication. They then share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes. The teacher collects a snapshot of predictions by asking learners to hold up fingers: 1 = very unsure, 5 = very confident, for each expression in turn. Predictions are left visible on a 'Before' sticky-note strip on the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the three expressions and the farm context using the board or printed cards. Say verbatim: 'Before we derive anything today, I want to know what your gut tells you. Use only what you already know about repeated multiplication — no new rules yet. You have three minutes of silent thinking.' [START 3-minute timer.] After individual time: 'Turn to your shoulder partner and compare your predictions. Do you agree? If not, whose reasoning is stronger?' [Allow 2 minutes.] Cold-call 3 pairs to share — one per expression. For each, ask: 'What multiplication story did you use to get there?' After sharing: 'Hold up fingers — how confident are you about (2^3)^2? … about 2^0? … about 2^(1/2)?' Record the class confidence distribution on the board next to each expression. Do NOT confirm or correct yet. Say: 'Keep these predictions live — we will return to them.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Activation of Prior Knowledge / Predict-Before-Observe: By requiring justification tied to repeated multiplication (the anchor representation established in Lesson 1), learners surface their existing mental models and make their reasoning visible. The confidence poll creates a public record of uncertainty that motivates the derivation activity and gives the teacher real-time formative data on which expression needs the most scaffolding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has a written numeric prediction AND a justification sentence for all three expressions before sharing begins. Teacher scans books during cold-call phase. Flag learners who have a number but no justification — prompt with: 'What multiplication did you picture?' The confidence distribution informs pacing: if fewer than half the class show 4–5 fingers for 2^(1/2), allocate extra derivation time in Phase 2.

framework.learnerExperience:
Learners work in groups of four on a structured 'Derivation Worksheet' that guides them to prove each rule from first principles using the quotient rule (a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n)) and expanded notation. The worksheet has three stations, each with a Kericho farm framing:

STATION A — Power Rule: Groups expand (2^3)^2 as repeated multiplication (write out all 6 twos), count the total factors, express as a single power, then generalise to (a^m)^n. They verify with (2^2)^3 and (3^2)^2.

STATION B — Negative Index Rule: Groups use the quotient rule to compute 2^3 ÷ 2^5, getting 2^(3−5) = 2^(−2). They also compute 8 ÷ 32 as a fraction and simplify. They reconcile the two answers, derive 2^(−2) = 1/2^2, then generalise to a^(−n) = 1/a^n. Farm framing: 'What does it mean for a plant to owe the farm two harvest cycles? Its net contribution is a fraction of the base amount.'

STATION C — Fractional Index Rule: Groups use the power rule in reverse: if (2^(1/2))^2 = 2^(1/2 × 2) = 2^1 = 2, then 2^(1/2) must be the number that, when multiplied by itself, gives 2 — i.e. √2. They verify with (2^(1/3))^3 and generalise to a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a. They then derive a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(a^m) = (ⁿ√a)^m. Farm framing: 'A half-harvest cycle of a tea plant yields 2^(1/2) grams — the geometric midpoint between 2^0 = 1 and 2^1 = 2.'

Each group records: the expanded working, the general rule, and one original farm sentence interpreting the rule.
framework.teacherMoves:
Distribute the Derivation Worksheet and say: 'Your job is to be mathematicians, not answer-receivers. Each station gives you a starting point — your group derives the rule. If you get stuck, the only hint I give is: go back to what the exponent means — repeated multiplication.' [Allow 15 minutes of group work.] Circulate and use targeted questions, NOT answers:
— Station A: 'How many twos total? Can you count them without writing them all out a second time?'
— Station B: 'You got 2^(−2) from the index law. You got 1/4 from ordinary arithmetic. What must 2^(−2) equal?'
— Station C: 'What is the question you are answering when you look for 2^(1/2)? Rephrase it as a square-root question.'
WAIT TIME: After posing each targeted question, wait at least 12 seconds before speaking again. After 15 minutes, conduct a gallery-style share: each group sends one 'ambassador' to stand at the next group's table and check their derivations. [3 minutes.] Reconvene whole class. Cold-call 3 different groups (one per station) to present their generalised rule and farm sentence. Write the three rules on the board in a 'Laws of Indices' reference box. Return to the Predict phase predictions and ask: 'How does your derivation change your original prediction?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Derive-Before-Tell (Guided Inquiry): Rather than presenting the rules and asking learners to apply them, learners construct the rules from the tools they already have (expanded notation + quotient rule). This mirrors the NGSS Science and Engineering Practice of 'Developing and Using Models' — the algebraic identity is the model, built from evidence (numeric examples). The gallery ambassador move ensures cross-group quality control and exposes learners to peer reasoning without full class disruption.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Every group's Station B working shows both the index-law route (2^(−2)) and the arithmetic route (1/4) reconciled with an equals sign — if not, the concept of negative indices as reciprocals has not landed. (2) Station C: learners write (2^(1/2))^2 = 2^1 as an intermediate step — if they jump straight to '√2' without this bridge, probe their reasoning. (3) During cold-call, listen for generalisations using variable bases (a, not just 2) — if all three groups stay numeric, prompt: 'Can you write that rule for any base a?'

framework.learnerExperience:
Learners apply the three new rules (plus the rules from Lessons 1–2) to a tiered set of problems, all framed within the Kericho tea farm and wider Kenyan contexts:

Tier 1 (all learners, 6 minutes, individual): Simplify: (a) (2^4)^3; (b) 5^(−2); (c) 9^(1/2); (d) 8^(2/3). For each, write the rule used.

Tier 2 (pairs, 6 minutes): A Kericho estate has 2^10 tea plants arranged in 2^(1/2) equal rows. Express the number of plants per row as a power of 2 and as a decimal (to 2 d.p.). Then: the estate manager wants to compare this estate with a smaller trial plot of 2^(−3) container-loads of tea. Explain in words what 2^(−3) container-loads means physically.

Tier 3 (extension, independent): A Nairobi food-processing company packages tea in tins whose volume is modelled by V = k^(3/2) cm³, where k is the base dimension in cm. If k = 16, find V. If V must equal 27 cm³, find k. Connect each calculation to the fractional index rule.

After individual/pair work, the teacher leads a whole-class 'rule audit': for each Tier 1 answer, the teacher writes a deliberate error on the board (e.g. (2^4)^3 = 2^7) and asks learners to identify and correct it, citing the specific rule.
framework.teacherMoves: Announce tiers clearly: 'Everyone starts on Tier 1 — you have 6 minutes, working alone. Tier 2 is in pairs. Tier 3 is a challenge for those who finish early.' [Set timer.] During Tier 1, circulate and mark correct/incorrect silently with a tick or a dot (not the answer). For Tier 2, listen specifically to how pairs articulate 2^(−3) container-loads — target the farm physical interpretation. After pair work, say: 'I have written four answers on the board. At least two are wrong. Your job as a class is to find the errors and explain exactly which rule was broken.' Read out each answer including errors. After WAIT TIME of 12 seconds, cold-call 4 different learners (rotate from those not yet called this lesson). For each correction, push with: 'Which rule? State it in words before you use symbols.' Close the explain phase by saying: 'The power rule, negative index rule, and fractional index rule are not new inventions — you derived them today from rules you already knew. That is what mathematicians do.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Error Analysis / Worked Example Critique (NGSS Practice: Constructing Explanations): Presenting deliberate errors shifts learners from passive answer-checking to active rule-enforcement. Requiring learners to name the rule in words before writing symbols deepens conceptual encoding. The tiered structure ensures all learners engage with the core rules while extension learners encounter the rules in a novel context (volume formula), foreshadowing Lesson 4's use of logarithms to solve for exponents.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Tier 1 — all four answers correct with rules cited: learner is ready for Tier 2/3. Any systematic error (e.g. consistently writing a^(m/n) = a^m / a^n instead of ⁿ√(a^m)) signals a conceptual gap to address before Lesson 4. (2) Tier 2 physical interpretation: if a learner writes '2^(−3) container-loads means a negative amount of tea,' this reveals the critical misconception that negative indices mean negative quantities — address immediately with a brief whole-class clarification using the reciprocal definition.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes on two sticky notes: one GREEN (something they now understand that was previously on the DQB as a question) and one ORANGE (a new question or remaining puzzle that today's lesson has raised). Examples likely to emerge: GREEN — 'Now I understand why 2^(−1) is 1/2, not −2 grams of tea'; ORANGE — 'If 2^(1/2) = √2, is there a way to find 2^(1/2) without a calculator using the logarithm table?'; 'What is 2^(π)?' Groups then physically move their Lesson 1–2 sticky notes on the class DQB from 'We wonder…' to 'We now know…' if those questions have been resolved, and add new notes. The class reads the updated DQB together and the teacher annotates the board to show the arc: Lessons 1–3 have established all six index laws; the ORANGE notes pointing toward logarithms and computation become the bridge to Lesson 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute two sticky notes per learner (pre-cut, green and orange). Say: 'Green = something you can now answer that was previously a wonder. Orange = a new question today's work has opened up. You have 3 minutes — silent, individual.' [3-minute timer.] After writing, ask 2 volunteers per colour to read their notes aloud before placing them on the DQB. Narrate the board update: 'Look at what we have resolved in three lessons — we have derived all six index laws from a single idea: repeated multiplication. Look at the orange notes — many of you are asking how to compute with these laws when numbers get large. That is exactly where we are going next.' Point explicitly to the phenomenon: 'Remember the Kericho farm manager who used a logarithm table to multiply large numbers in two minutes? We now have the index laws that make that possible. Next lesson, we find out how.' Write on the DQB in a new column: 'Lesson 4 will address: using logarithms to compute with large powers.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as Epistemic Artefact: The DQB is not decorative — it is a living record of the class's collective knowledge state. The green/orange protocol makes the distinction between resolved knowledge and productive uncertainty explicit and public. Narrating the arc from phenomenon → index laws → logarithms gives learners a sense of purposeful progression, maintaining motivation across the 8-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: Green notes should reference specific rules (power, negative, or fractional index) with a connection to the phenomenon — a generic 'I understand indices better' is insufficient; prompt the learner to be specific. Orange notes should be genuine mathematical questions, not restatements of content already covered — if a learner's orange note is 'What is the product rule?', they have missed learning from Lessons 1–2 and need targeted follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative 'Index Laws Model' — a two-column graphic organiser started in Lesson 1, with columns labelled 'Law (symbolic)' and 'Kericho Farm Meaning.' They add three new rows for today's rules. For each row, they must: (1) write the symbolic rule; (2) write a specific numeric example using powers of 2; (3) write one sentence connecting the rule to the tea farm phenomenon. After completing their own model (6 minutes individual), learners share with their group and negotiate a 'best farm sentence' for the fractional index rule — the most conceptually challenging. One sentence per group is written on a shared chart paper strip and displayed on the classroom wall under the heading: '2^(1/2) means… (Class consensus).' The lesson closes with the teacher reading two or three of the displayed sentences aloud and affirming the key insight: a fractional index is a root, and a root is the inverse of a power — a relationship that logarithms will generalise to all bases in the next lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Index Laws Model from Lesson 1. We are adding three rows today — power rule, negative index rule, and fractional index rule. You have 6 minutes to complete all three rows individually. The symbolic rule and numeric example are non-negotiable. The farm sentence is where you show real understanding.' [6-minute timer, circulate.] After individual work: 'In your groups, read your fractional index farm sentences aloud. Vote on the clearest and most accurate one. Write it on the chart strip.' [3 minutes.] Gallery walk: learners read two other groups' strips (2 minutes). Whole class: cold-call 2 groups to read and defend their sentence. Teacher closes: 'Your model now holds all six index laws. Every one of them came from one idea — what does it mean to multiply a number by itself repeatedly? In Lesson 4, we will add a new column to this model: what the logarithm table does with each of these laws. Keep your model safe — it is your reference for the rest of this unit.' Assign homework: 'Using your model, create two original index expressions — one requiring the negative index rule and one requiring the fractional index rule — set in any Kenyan context of your choice (market prices, population, farming, athletics). Bring them to Lesson 4.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (NGSS Practice: Developing and Using Models): The graphic organiser is a personal, evolving model that learners build across all 8 lessons. Each lesson's contribution is visible, making learning progression concrete. The group negotiation of the 'best farm sentence' for 2^(1/2) requires learners to evaluate precision and meaning simultaneously — a higher-order sensemaking demand. The wall display creates a shared class artefact that can be referenced in every subsequent lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The symbolic rule must be correct and generalised (using a and n, not just 2 and 3). (2) The numeric example must be correct and use the rule, not a simpler shortcut. (3) The farm sentence must use the word 'harvest' or 'plant' or 'container' AND correctly interpret the index operation — not just restate the symbolic rule in words. A sentence like '2^(−2) means the exponent is negative' scores zero; '2^(−2) means the farm produces 1/4 of a base container-load — it is the reciprocal of 2^2 = 4 container-loads' scores full marks. Collect 6 randomly selected model pages at the end of the lesson for written feedback.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider the following questions: (1) DERIVATION DEPTH — Did learners genuinely derive the three rules, or did they reverse-engineer from a remembered answer? Evidence: check whether Station C worksheets show the intermediate step (2^(1/2))^2 = 2^1 before stating 2^(1/2) = √2. If this step is missing, plan a brief re-derivation warm-up at the start of Lesson 4. (2) FRACTIONAL INDEX CONCEPTUAL GAP — The fractional index rule is the most cognitively demanding of the three. How many learners in the exit model could write a farm sentence that correctly distinguishes 2^(1/2) as a root (not half of 2)? If fewer than 70% achieved this, open Lesson 4 with a 5-minute targeted re-engagement using a concrete example: 'What length of a square has area 2 cm²?' (3) NEGATIVE INDEX MISCONCEPTION — Did any learners persist in interpreting 2^(−n) as a negative quantity rather than a reciprocal? This misconception is high-stakes because it will corrupt logarithm work in Lessons 5–7. Plan individual follow-up before Lesson 4 for any learner whose Tier 2 Kericho interpretation used 'negative tea.' (4) DQB QUALITY — Are the orange sticky notes pointing toward logarithms, computation, or inverse operations? If the orange notes are mostly about index simplification (content already taught), learners may not yet see the larger arc of the unit — revisit the phenomenon story at the start of Lesson 4 to re-anchor. (5) PACING — If the derivation phase ran over time, note which station caused the delay (most likely Station C). Consider providing a partially completed Station C scaffold for lower-attaining groups in future iterations while keeping Stations A and B fully open. (6) HOMEWORK QUALITY CHECK — At the start of Lesson 4, cold-call 3 learners to share their original index expressions. Use these as the warm-up context for introducing logarithms, thereby honoring learner-generated content and reinforcing the Kenya-context rule.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed (through their own group derivations) that: (1) raising a power to another power multiplies the exponents — (2^3)^2 = 2^6 = 64, confirmed by writing out all six factors of 2; (2) applying the quotient rule to a case where the denominator exponent exceeds the numerator (e.g. 2^3 ÷ 2^5 = 2^(−2) = 1/4) reveals that negative indices produce reciprocal fractions; (3) using the power rule in reverse, 2^(1/2) must be the number whose square is 2, i.e. √2 ≈ 1.414 — meaning a 'half harvest cycle' yields the geometric mean between 2^0 and 2^1.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned and can now state: (1) Power Rule — (a^m)^n = a^(mn); (2) Negative Index Rule — a^(−n) = 1/a^n, so a negative exponent signals a reciprocal, NOT a negative quantity; (3) Fractional Index Rule — a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a and a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(a^m) = (ⁿ√a)^m. Together with the product rule, quotient rule, and zero index rule from Lessons 1–2, learners now hold the complete set of six index laws, all derived from the single foundational idea of repeated multiplication.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained: (1) why the Kericho tea farm manager's harvest figures grow exponentially — each additional power of 2 doubles production, and the power rule explains why scaling an already-scaled estate multiplies the exponent; (2) why 2^(−3) container-loads does not mean 'negative tea' but means the farm is 1/8 of a reference container-load — a physically meaningful fraction relevant when comparing micro-plots to large estates; (3) why 2^(1/2) grams per 'half harvest cycle' is approximately 1.414 grams — the geometric midpoint of the doubling sequence — and how this connects roots to indices, foreshadowing logarithms as the tool for reversing any index operation.

LESSONS.title: Introduction to Common Logarithms: Definition, Characteristic, Mantissa, and Reading Four-Figure Tables

slo.purpose: Learners are formally introduced to the definition of a common logarithm (log₁₀ x = n ↔ 10ⁿ = x), identify the characteristic and mantissa of a logarithm, and practise reading four-figure logarithm tables for numbers from 1 to 9,999 — connecting this tool directly to the Kericho tea-farm phenomenon and the driving question about making unwieldy numbers manageable.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) state and apply the definition log₁₀ x = n ↔ 10ⁿ = x; (b) evaluate common logarithms of exact powers of 10 (including negative powers) without tables; (c) identify and state the characteristic and mantissa of any common logarithm; (d) read the mantissa of a four-figure logarithm table correctly for numbers between 1 and 9,999.
slo.skills: Reading and interpreting four-figure mathematical tables; translating between exponential and logarithmic form; decomposing a logarithm into its integer characteristic and decimal mantissa; applying the pH supporting phenomenon to evaluate negative-characteristic logarithms.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that logarithms are not abstract tricks but a historically proven computational tool — the same tool that helped Kenyan agronomists and engineers long before calculators existed — and develop confidence in reading mathematical tables accurately.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use logarithms in computations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3 learners established index notation and the laws of indices, and saw in the phenomenon that the tea-farm manager struggled with large-number multiplication. Lesson 4 is the pivot: learners now receive the formal definition of log₁₀ and discover that a logarithm is simply the exponent they already know — rewritten. By the end of this lesson they can pick up a four-figure table and read a mantissa, equipping them for Lesson 5 (multiplication and division via logs) and directly answering the phenomenon's puzzle of 'how can adding two small decimals equal multiplying two enormous numbers?'
slo.safetyNotes: No chemical or physical hazards. If the pH supporting phenomenon is demonstrated with litmus paper or universal indicator and lemon/lime juice (optional), ensure learners do not ingest any substance. Handle glass containers with care. Standard classroom safety applies.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting what log₁₀ 1,000 means before any instruction. A short supporting phenomenon — pH values of common Kenyan foods and drinks (lemon juice, uji, milk, lake water from Lake Victoria) — provides a memorable, concrete context for negative-characteristic logarithms. The teacher formally defines the common logarithm, guides learners through converting between exponential and log form, and introduces the characteristic–mantissa decomposition. Learners then work in pairs to practise reading a physical four-figure logarithm table for at least eight numbers, recording results on a structured table-reading worksheet. The lesson closes with DQB updating and a cumulative model revision connecting logarithms back to the tea-farm phenomenon.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-sheet with three prompt questions written on the board: (1) 'The Kericho tea estate produces 10³ kg of tea. Write 10³ as an ordinary number. Now write it in words.' (2) 'If 10ⁿ = 1,000, what is n? What is 10ⁿ = 0.01, what is n?' (3) 'The fellow farmer in our phenomenon said he used a table of logarithms. Write down, in your own words, what you think a logarithm IS — even if you have never been taught.' Learners write individual predictions silently for 5 minutes, then share with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes. No judgement is given — all predictions are valid starting points. Selected predictions are pinned to the Driving Question Board under the column 'What we THINK we know about logs.'
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon recap slide: 'The fellow farmer opened a four-figure table and looked up two numbers. He added them. He got the total tea production. HOW?' SAY: 'Before I teach you anything about logarithms today, I want to know what YOU already think they are. You have 5 minutes — write on your half-sheet.' Set a visible timer. After 5 minutes, say: 'Turn to your shoulder partner and share your answer to question 2 — what is n when 10ⁿ = 0.01?' Allow 2 minutes pair discussion. Cold-call 3 learners using name sticks: ask each 'What did you and your partner decide — and WHY?' Apply 12-second wait time after each response before probing. Do NOT correct yet — record predictions on the board in two columns: 'n is positive' and 'n is negative / zero.' SAY: 'Hold those ideas. By the end of today you will know exactly why n must be negative for 0.01 — and that fact is the key to understanding the pH of your morning uji.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-and-Record Prediction Strategy: by surfacing prior conceptions (including misconceptions) about exponents and logarithms before instruction, the teacher creates cognitive dissonance that motivates the formal definition. Recording predictions visibly on the board signals that student thinking is valued and creates a reference point for revision at lesson end.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learners can write a numerical value for n when 10ⁿ = 1,000 (expected: n = 3). Teacher scans half-sheets during pair-share; if fewer than 60% correctly identify n = 3, the teacher pauses and re-asks: 'We did index notation in Lesson 1 — what does the small raised 3 mean in 10³?' before proceeding. Note any learner who correctly writes n = −2 for 10ⁿ = 0.01 — this learner will be invited to explain their reasoning during Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Supporting Phenomenon — The pH Scale of Kenyan Foods. The teacher displays a large visual poster (or projected slide) showing a pH strip with the following real Kenyan data points labelled: lemon juice (pH ≈ 2), uji/fermented porridge (pH ≈ 3.5), milk from a Rift Valley dairy (pH ≈ 6.8), clean water from Lake Naivasha (pH ≈ 7), and bleaching agent used on Mombasa dhow sails (pH ≈ 12). Alongside each food, the HYDROGEN ION CONCENTRATION [H⁺] is written in full: lemon juice = 0.01 mol/L, uji ≈ 0.000316 mol/L, etc. Learners observe that chemists defined pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. A second visual shows the same data as a number line of powers of 10: 10⁻², 10⁻³·⁵, 10⁻⁶·⁸ etc. Learners complete an Observation Table (on their worksheet) with three columns: Food/Liquid | [H⁺] written as a power of 10 | pH value. They notice that pH is simply the magnitude of the exponent — i.e., the logarithm — of the concentration. A 3-minute silent reading excerpt (one paragraph, on the worksheet) explains: 'John Napier invented logarithms in 1614. Kenyan scientists like agrochemists at the Tea Research Foundation in Kericho use pH — a logarithmic scale — to test whether soil acidity is suitable for tea growing. Tea grows best at pH 4.5–5.5. A change of 1 pH unit means the hydrogen ion concentration changes by a factor of 10.' Learners annotate the excerpt, underlining what connects to the phenomenon.
framework.teacherMoves: Post or project the pH poster before learners enter. As lesson starts, point to lemon juice row: 'Naomi, read the [H⁺] value for lemon juice aloud.' After response, SAY: 'Now write that as a power of 10 in your observation table. You have 30 seconds.' Cold-call a second learner: 'David, what power of 10 did you write?' After response and 12-second wait: 'Everyone check — did you write 10⁻²? Thumbs up if yes.' Address any thumbs-down by asking: 'What did you write instead? Let us see why 0.01 = 10⁻².' Reference Lesson 2 (negative indices): '0.01 = 1/100 = 1/10² = 10⁻² — this is a law we already proved.' Continue row by row for 6 minutes, alternating cold-calls (target: every learner called at least once across the table). After the table is complete, SAY: 'Now read the excerpt silently and underline ONE sentence that surprises you. 3 minutes.' After reading, cold-call 2 learners: 'Faith, what surprised you?' Apply 15-second wait. Conclude Observe phase: 'What you have just noticed — that pH IS the exponent — is exactly the definition of a logarithm. That is what we formalise now.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Anchored Observation with Real Data: using authentic Kenyan pH data grounds the abstract concept of logarithms in a tangible, memorable context. By physically writing [H⁺] as powers of 10 and then reading off the pH, learners are constructing the logarithm relationship themselves before it is named — a form of guided inquiry aligned with NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) adapted for mathematics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: completed Observation Table with correct powers of 10 for at least 4 of 5 rows. Teacher circulates during table completion; specifically check whether learners correctly write the negative sign in 10⁻² (common omission). If a learner writes 10² instead of 10⁻², ask: 'Is 0.01 greater or less than 1? What does that tell us about the sign of the exponent?' — do NOT simply correct; elicit reasoning.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A — Formal Definition (10 min). The teacher writes on the board: 'log₁₀ x = n  ↔  10ⁿ = x' and reads it aloud twice. Learners copy this into their notes with a box around it. Three worked examples are displayed and completed together: (1) log₁₀ 1,000 = ? → 10? = 1,000 → ? = 3; (2) log₁₀ 0.01 = ? → 10? = 0.01 → ? = −2; (3) log₁₀ 1 = ? → 10? = 1 → ? = 0. Learners then individually complete a six-item rapid conversion table (exponential → log form and log → exponential form) on their worksheet. Part B — Characteristic and Mantissa (12 min). Teacher introduces the decomposition: any common logarithm = characteristic (integer part, can be negative) + mantissa (decimal part, always 0 ≤ mantissa < 1). Using the examples log₁₀ 3,500 ≈ 3.5441: characteristic = 3 (because 1,000 ≤ 3,500 < 10,000, i.e., 10³ ≤ 3,500 < 10⁴), mantissa = 0.5441 (read from table). Kenyan context: 'The tea estate in Kericho ships 3,500 kg per container. log₁₀ 3,500 = 3.5441. The characteristic 3 tells us there are 4 digits — the mantissa 0.5441 gives the precision.' Learners practise identifying the characteristic from the number of digits for eight numbers on their worksheet without using tables. Part C — Reading Four-Figure Tables (18 min). Each pair receives a physical four-figure logarithm table booklet (or a printed A3 extract). Teacher models on the board: 'To find log₁₀ 356: (1) The characteristic is 2 (3 digits). (2) Look up row 35, column 6 in the table → mantissa = 0.5514. (3) Therefore log₁₀ 356 = 2.5514.' Learners then work in pairs to look up and record log values for: 47, 520, 8.3, 1,200, 0.064 (teacher guides characteristic of the last two), 73.5, 9.99, and 3,142 (π × 1,000 — Kenyan connection to circular tea plantation design). Each pair records their values in a structured Table-Reading Record on the worksheet.
framework.teacherMoves: Part A: Write the definition slowly, narrating each symbol: 'The small 10 here is the BASE. The n is the EXPONENT — the POWER. This is the same power we have been writing since Lesson 1.' After worked example 2, SAY: 'Remind me — we saw 10⁻² in the pH table. What food had [H⁺] = 10⁻²?' (Wait 10 seconds — expected: lemon juice.) 'Exactly. So log₁₀ 0.01 = −2 is just saying: lemon juice has a hydrogen ion concentration that is 10 to the NEGATIVE 2. Logarithm and pH are the same mathematics.' Cold-call the learner identified in Phase 1 who wrote n = −2 correctly: 'You predicted this in your half-sheet — explain to the class how you knew.' After the six-item rapid conversion, ask learners to self-mark using the answer key projected for 60 seconds. Ask: 'Raise your hand if you got all six correct.' Then: 'Raise your hand if you got five.' Address the most common error. Part B: After modelling characteristic of 3,500, SAY: 'Here is the rule without a table: the characteristic of a number ≥ 1 is one less than the number of digits before the decimal point. Write that rule in a box in your notes.' Give 2 minutes for the eight-item worksheet. Cold-call 3 learners for answers, applying 12-second wait each time. Part C: Model the table lookup TWICE at full speed, narrating every step. Then say: 'Now you and your partner do the same for 47. I will walk around — you have 3 minutes. I must see BOTH partners' fingers on the table simultaneously.' Circulate and check hand positions on the table. After 8 numbers are complete, cold-call one pair per number to share their answer. Record all 8 on the board. SAY: 'Look at the last entry — 3,142. That is π × 1,000. Agronomists at KALRO in Nairobi sometimes compute the circumference of a circular test plantation — now you can find the logarithm of that number in under 20 seconds.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept-Definition-Application Cycle (CDA) with Phenomenon Anchoring: the teacher first formalises the concept (log definition), then builds the structural sub-concept (characteristic + mantissa), then immediately applies it to the procedural skill (table reading) — each step re-anchored to the Kericho tea phenomenon or the pH supporting phenomenon. This prevents the definition from floating free of meaning. NGSS Practice 6 (Constructing Explanations) is embedded as learners articulate in writing why the characteristic of 3,500 is 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Three checkpoints: (1) Six-item rapid conversion self-mark — teacher notes class accuracy rate. If >25% miss items involving negative logs (e.g., log₁₀ 0.001), pause and reteach using the pH table before moving to Part B. (2) Eight-item characteristic identification — teacher collects three randomly selected worksheets and checks during pair work; any learner writing characteristic = (number of digits) rather than (digits − 1) is flagged for targeted support. (3) Table-reading record — teacher verifies log₁₀ 47 = 1.6721 ± 0.0001 and log₁₀ 520 = 2.7160 ± 0.0001 as a quick accuracy check; pairs with both values correct are considered fluent; pairs with errors are re-shown the table structure.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board. In pairs, they write two sticky notes: (A) one GREEN note titled 'What we NOW know' — must include at least one sentence using the words 'characteristic,' 'mantissa,' and 'four-figure table'; (B) one ORANGE note titled 'New question raised' — a genuine question that this lesson has created about using logs in the tea-farm calculation. Pairs post their notes on the DQB. The teacher reads 3–4 orange notes aloud and previews: 'Lesson 5 will answer exactly THIS question — how do we multiply two large numbers using the log table we just learned to read?'. The class reviews the original prediction sticky notes from Phase 1 and learners physically move any note they now believe to be correct from the 'What we THINK' column to the 'What we KNOW' column.
framework.teacherMoves: Give pairs 4 minutes for sticky notes. As they write, circulate and prompt any pair whose green note lacks mathematical precision: 'Can you write the actual definition — log₁₀ x = n means…?' Post the notes quickly. Read 3 orange 'new question' notes aloud, naming the pair: 'Amina and Koech ask — if you can use logs to multiply, can you use them to divide too? Excellent question. Keep it on the board.' Point to the original Phase 1 predictions: 'Look at our board from the start of the lesson. Which of these predictions were right? Let us move them.' Guide this physically — do not simply announce answers. SAY: 'The driving question asks how logarithms help the tea farmer. Today's lesson gave us the key that unlocks that question — we now know WHAT a logarithm is. Next lesson we use it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Progressive DQB Revision Strategy: the physical act of moving sticky notes from 'think' to 'know' externalises metacognitive growth. The orange 'new question' notes ensure learners are not passive recipients but active generators of the next inquiry step — directly aligned with KICD's emphasis on learner-centred, inquiry-based pedagogy and NGSS Practice 1 (Asking Questions).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: every green sticky note must contain the log definition in symbolic form (log₁₀ x = n ↔ 10ⁿ = x) or an equivalent statement. Teacher checks notes as they are posted; any note missing the symbolic definition is returned to the pair with the prompt: 'Show me the mathematical relationship — not just the words.' Count of orange notes mentioning multiplication/division (expected: majority) confirms learners have grasped the lesson's connective role in the storyline.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their cumulative unit model — a two-column poster begun in Lesson 1 with the headings 'INDEX SIDE' and 'LOGARITHM SIDE.' In Lessons 1–3 they populated the INDEX SIDE with: repeated multiplication → index notation → laws of indices → tea-farm harvest calculation in index form. Today they begin populating the LOGARITHM SIDE for the first time. Using a guided model-revision template on their worksheet, each learner adds: (1) the formal definition box (log₁₀ x = n ↔ 10ⁿ = x) with an arrow connecting it to '10³ = 1,000' already on the INDEX SIDE; (2) a characteristic-mantissa decomposition diagram for log₁₀ 3,500 = 3.5441 (annotated with what each part means in the tea-farm context); (3) a 'bridge statement' in their own words: 'A logarithm is the EXPONENT, rewritten on the left side of the equation. The four-figure table gives me the mantissa of that exponent for any number I choose.' Finally, learners sketch a simple arrow diagram showing: LARGE NUMBER → log table → LOGARITHM (char + mantissa) → [to be completed in Lesson 5: → ADD logs → antilog → PRODUCT]. The last two boxes are left blank with a dotted outline labelled 'Lesson 5.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the model-revision template or direct learners to their cumulative poster. SAY: 'Your model so far lives entirely on the INDEX SIDE. Today we open the LOGARITHM SIDE. This is the moment the fellow farmer's trick starts to make sense.' Give 8 minutes for individual model revision. Circulate and look for three things: (a) the bidirectional arrow between log definition and the index notation already in the model; (b) correct labelling of characteristic vs. mantissa; (c) the bridge statement in the learner's own words. After 8 minutes, ask two volunteers to read their bridge statement aloud. After each, ask the class: 'Does that bridge statement capture what we learned? Thumbs up / sideways / down.' Use sideways thumbs as a prompt: 'What would you add or change?' Close with: 'The dotted boxes you left blank are the payoff of this entire unit. In Lesson 5, you will fill them in — and when you do, you will have solved the tea-farm manager's problem completely.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Conceptual Model Revision (CCMR): maintaining a single evolving model across all 8 lessons makes the conceptual architecture of the unit visible. By leaving Lesson 5 boxes deliberately blank, the teacher creates productive anticipation (a 'conceptual cliffhanger') and signals that today's content is a necessary — but incomplete — piece of a larger explanation. This directly mirrors NGSS Practice 2 (Developing and Using Models).
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit Task (final 3 minutes): each learner individually writes on the back of their worksheet: 'Without using a table, state log₁₀ 10,000 and give the characteristic and mantissa of log₁₀ 2,500 (hint: characteristic only — no table needed for characteristic).' Expected responses: log₁₀ 10,000 = 4; characteristic of log₁₀ 2,500 = 3 (four digits before decimal point, minus 1). Teacher collects these as the learners leave. Any learner who cannot state log₁₀ 10,000 = 4 will receive a five-minute review at the start of Lesson 5 connecting 10⁴ = 10,000 back to the index laws.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record brief notes in your lesson record book:
1. DEFINITION FLUENCY: Could learners move fluently between exponential form and logarithmic form (both directions) during the six-item rapid conversion? If more than 25% struggled, consider opening Lesson 5 with a two-minute 'log ↔ exponential' oral drill before proceeding to multiplication using logs.
2. NEGATIVE CHARACTERISTICS: Did learners correctly handle log₁₀ 0.01 = −2 and relate it to the pH phenomenon? Confusion about negative characteristics is the most common block that will impede Lesson 6 (division using logarithms of numbers less than 1). If confusion persists, use the lemon-juice pH anchor ('the farmer tests soil pH 4.5 — what is [H⁺]?') as a re-entry point.
3. TABLE-READING FLUENCY: Were both members of each pair using their fingers on the physical table simultaneously (as instructed)? Passive partners often become lost when table reading advances to anti-logarithms in Lesson 5. Identify pairs where only one learner is doing the table work and restructure pairs if needed.
4. DQB QUALITY: Did the orange 'new question' sticky notes show genuine forward curiosity about multiplication/division via logs, or were they superficial? Shallow orange notes suggest learners have not yet connected today's definition lesson to the phenomenon's unanswered puzzle. If so, re-read the phenomenon aloud at the start of Lesson 5 and explicitly ask: 'The fellow farmer added two numbers from a table. TODAY we learn what he added — and why adding works.'
5. MODEL COHERENCE: Check three randomly selected cumulative models for the bidirectional arrow connecting the log definition on the LOGARITHM SIDE to the existing index notation on the INDEX SIDE. This arrow is the conceptual spine of the unit. If it is missing, the learner has not yet grasped that a logarithm IS an exponent — the central insight of this lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed a pH data table featuring common Kenyan foods and liquids (lemon juice, uji, Rift Valley dairy milk, Lake Naivasha water) in which hydrogen ion concentrations were expressed as negative powers of 10. They noticed that the pH value of each substance equals the magnitude of the exponent of its [H⁺] concentration, and that a change of 1 pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in concentration — mirroring the tea-farm phenomenon where changing an exponent by 1 doubles the harvest.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned the formal definition of the common logarithm: log₁₀ x = n if and only if 10ⁿ = x. They learned to decompose any common logarithm into its characteristic (the integer part, equal to one less than the number of digits before the decimal point for numbers ≥ 1) and its mantissa (the non-negative decimal part, read from a four-figure table). They practised reading the mantissa from a physical four-figure logarithm table for eight numbers including 3,142 (π × 1,000, connected to circular plantation geometry).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained that the logarithm is simply the exponent rewritten on the left side of the equation — the same exponent they have been working with since Lesson 1 in index notation. They articulated why the characteristic of log₁₀ 3,500 is 3 (because 10³ ≤ 3,500 < 10⁴) and connected the negative-characteristic logarithm log₁₀ 0.01 = −2 to the pH phenomenon (lemon juice [H⁺] = 10⁻² mol/L). They began populating the LOGARITHM SIDE of their cumulative unit model and left the 'add logs → antilog → product' boxes blank as a bridge to Lesson 5.
