LESSONS.title: Using Mathematical Tables and Calculators for Logarithms and Antilogarithms
LESSONS.aresKeywords: common logarithms, four-figure tables, antilogarithms, mantissa, characteristic

slo.purpose: Students build systematic fluency in reading both logarithm and antilogarithm tables, and cross-check every result with a scientific calculator, using M-Pesa transaction volumes as the source of large numbers — advancing the unit's central question of how logarithms convert unwieldy multiplication into simple addition.
slo.knowledge:
• State that the antilogarithm of x is 10ˣ, and that antilog tables reverse the process of log tables
• Explain the role of the characteristic in placing the decimal point when finding an antilogarithm
• Describe the full table-reading procedure for both log and antilog tables, including use of the difference columns
• Recognise that a scientific calculator's log and 10ˣ (or INV log) keys give the same results as four-figure tables, to four significant figures
slo.skills:
• Read a four-figure logarithm table to find log₁₀ N for any N between 1 and 9999, using the mean-difference columns correctly
• Read a four-figure antilogarithm table to find 10ˣ for any x between 0 and 0.9999, and apply the characteristic to position the decimal point
• Use a scientific calculator to verify log₁₀ N and 10ˣ values and reconcile minor rounding differences
• Apply the full log → operation → antilog workflow to a multiplication problem drawn from the M-Pesa phenomenon
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematical tables are a powerful, universally accessible tool — usable even without electricity — mirroring the Kericho farmer's ability to compute without a calculator
• Show precision and patience in reading tables, recognising that a one-digit error in the difference column can produce a large error in the final answer
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use logarithms in computations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1–4 established what logarithms are and how to find the log of a number. Lesson 5 completes the two-way journey: students can now move from number → logarithm (log table) AND from logarithm → number (antilog table). This unlocks the full computational chain — log, operate, antilog — that the Kericho farmer's colleague used to multiply enormous harvest figures in under two minutes, and that the M-Pesa supporting phenomenon makes viscerally real.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. Ensure scientific calculators have charged batteries or are solar-powered. If shared devices are used, establish a clear rotation protocol so all learners get hands-on calculator time.

LESSONS.overview:
Lesson 5 sits at the pivot point of the unit: students have learned what logarithms are and how to read a log table (Lesson 4); now they learn the reverse — the antilogarithm — and practise the complete log-table workflow end to end. The lesson opens with a striking M-Pesa statistic: Safaricom's network processes approximately 1.7 × 10⁷ transactions every single day across Kenya. A farm manager in Kericho receiving payment for a tea shipment, or a maize trader in Eldoret settling a bulk order, is one node in that vast network. The teacher poses the puzzle: if you know that log₁₀ x = 7.2304, what is x? Students have not yet seen antilogarithm tables, so this question deliberately sits just beyond their current reach — creating the productive tension that drives the Observe phase.

In the Observe phase the teacher models, with narrated think-aloud and explicit wait-time, the complete four-step procedure: (1) separate the characteristic from the mantissa; (2) locate the mantissa row and column in the antilog table; (3) add the mean-difference correction; (4) use the characteristic to place the decimal point. Students then practise four carefully graded problems — two logarithm lookups and two antilogarithm lookups — cross-checking each answer on a scientific calculator. The M-Pesa transaction volume, the Kericho tea estate total yield, and daily milk output figures from Nyandarua county dairy cooperatives supply the numbers, keeping every calculation anchored in a recognisable Kenyan economic context.

The Explain phase requires students to articulate, in writing and in paired discussion, why the antilog is the inverse of the log, connecting it to the index definition log₁₀ x = n ⟺ 10ⁿ = x established in Lesson 4. The Driving Question Board is updated to record that students can now complete the full log → add/subtract → antilog chain — the very procedure that puzzled them in the anchoring phenomenon — even if they have not yet formally proved the log laws that justify the addition step. The Model Building phase revises the cumulative unit model to show the two-way arrow between numbers and logarithms, making explicit that the antilog table is simply a table of powers of 10.

framework.learnerExperience: Students read a single prompt displayed on the board: 'Safaricom's M-Pesa processed roughly 17,000,000 transactions yesterday. A data analyst writes in her notebook: log₁₀(17,000,000) ≈ 7.2304. Her supervisor asks: given only the number 7.2304, how would you recover the original 17,000,000 without a calculator?' Students write a one-sentence prediction in their exercise books, then share with a partner for 60 seconds. The teacher then poses a second, sharper question: 'In Lesson 4 we moved from a number to its logarithm. Can we go the other way — from a logarithm back to the number? What tool or method do you think exists for that?' Students record their prediction before any instruction begins.
framework.teacherMoves: Write the M-Pesa prompt on the board before learners enter the room. After learners settle, say: 'Read the board silently and write your prediction — do not discuss yet. You have 90 seconds.' [WAIT 90 seconds — circulate to note the range of ideas without commenting.] Call on 3 learners by name (cold-call): 'Achieng, what did you write?' → 'Mutua, yours?' → 'Wanjiru, anything different?' After each response, say only 'Thank you — hold that idea.' Do NOT confirm or correct. Then say: 'Today we are going to discover the tool that lets us reverse the logarithm. By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at 7.2304 and recover 17,000,000 — and you will understand exactly why that works.' Record the three student predictions on a corner of the board under the heading 'Our Predictions' — they will be revisited at the DQB phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Anchored Uncertainty — Students activate prior knowledge (log definition from Lesson 4, index notation from Lessons 1–3) to predict a procedure they have not yet seen. The deliberate choice of an M-Pesa number that is large and familiar (every student has observed family members use M-Pesa) ensures the problem feels real and motivates resolution. Recording predictions publicly commits students to an intellectual position they will later revise, supporting metacognitive awareness.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans written predictions during the 90-second wait. Look for: (a) students who write 'reverse the process / undo the log' — these show strong conceptual readiness; (b) students who write 'divide by 10 somehow' — these reveal additive rather than exponential thinking, flagging a misconception to address in the Explain phase; (c) blank pages — these students need a re-read prompt: 'Write anything you know about 10 raised to a power of 7.' Record names in the two latter categories for targeted questioning in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher distributes (or projects) a four-figure antilogarithm table alongside the four-figure logarithm table used in Lesson 4. Students observe a narrated, step-by-step teacher demonstration of two worked examples — one log lookup and one antilog lookup — using numbers drawn from the M-Pesa and Kericho tea contexts. Students do NOT copy during the demonstration; they observe and annotate a printed skeleton framework provided on a half-sheet. After the demonstration, students attempt four practice problems in pairs, recording each step in the four-row skeleton (characteristic | mantissa row | column + difference | final answer), then verify each answer by pressing the log or 10ˣ key on a scientific calculator.
framework.teacherMoves:
DEMONSTRATION — WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (Log lookup): Write on board: 'Find log₁₀(5,840) using the four-figure table.' Say: 'Watch the four steps — I will name each step as I do it.' Step 1 — 'I identify the significant figures: 5, 8, 4, 0. I ignore trailing zeros for the mantissa.' Step 2 — 'Characteristic: 5840 has 4 digits before the decimal, so characteristic = 4 − 1 = 3.' Step 3 — 'I go to row 58 in the log table, then column 4. I read 7招 — let me read aloud: 7招, that is 7 6 6 9.' [Point to cell visibly.] Step 4 — 'The difference column for the next digit — here there is no fifth digit, so difference = 0. Mantissa = 0.7669. Therefore log₁₀(5840) = 3.7669.' Ask: 'Kariuki, what would the characteristic be if the number were 58.4 instead?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call 1. Then: 'Otieno, what if it were 0.584?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 2.

DEMONSTRATION — WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (Antilog lookup): Write on board: 'Find antilog(7.2304) — that is, find x where log₁₀ x = 7.2304.' Say: 'This is the M-Pesa reversal question from our prediction.' Step 1 — 'Separate: characteristic = 7, mantissa = 0.2304.' Step 2 — 'Open the antilog table. Look up row .23 — the first two decimal places.' Step 3 — 'Column for third decimal digit: 0. Read the cell: I get 1 6 9 8.' Step 4 — 'Fourth decimal digit is 4 — go to the mean-difference column for 4: I add 2. So antilog of .2304 = 1698 + 2 = 1700.' Step 5 — 'Characteristic = 7 means the answer has 7+1 = 8 digits before the decimal point. So x = 1.700 × 10⁷ = 17,000,000.' Say: 'That is the 17 million M-Pesa transactions — we recovered the original number!' [WAIT 8 seconds for the class to absorb.] 

PRACTICE — distribute half-sheets. Say: 'In pairs, complete problems A through D on your skeleton sheet. For each one: (1) write the four steps, (2) write the calculator verification. You have 9 minutes.' Problems: A. log₁₀(3,240) [Kericho tea estate daily output in kg]; B. log₁₀(47.6) [price per kg of processed tea in KSh]; C. antilog(4.5922) [total M-Pesa value in KSh × 10⁴]; D. antilog(2.8751) [number of tea bags packed per shift at a Limuru factory]. Circulate; when a pair is stuck, prompt: 'Which step are you on? Read the step name aloud.' Do not give the answer. After 9 minutes, cold-call 4 different pairs (one per problem) to read their four steps aloud. [WAIT 8 seconds between each cold-call and the next.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Annotated Worked Example with Skeleton Framework — The skeleton framework (four named rows) prevents passive copying while structuring observation. By naming each procedural step ('characteristic,' 'mantissa row,' 'column,' 'difference'), the teacher makes the tacit structure of table-reading explicit and transferable. The immediate calculator cross-check creates a self-correcting feedback loop: if the table answer and the calculator answer differ by more than 1 in the last digit, students know they made a reading error and must retrace their steps rather than simply accepting an incorrect answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: While pairs work, teacher looks for: (1) students writing the characteristic as the number of digits (instead of digits minus 1) — ask 'How many digits does 3,240 have? So what is one less than that?'; (2) students reading the antilog row from the log table instead of the antilog table — point to the table title; (3) calculator answers that differ from table answers by more than 2 in the last place — ask the pair to re-read the difference column. Collect four skeleton sheets at random after the cold-call presentations to check step-level recording quality before the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Students individually answer three 'Explain It' prompts in their exercise books (2 minutes writing, then 3-minute paired comparison): Prompt 1 — 'Why is the antilogarithm table described as a table of powers of 10? Use the definition log₁₀ x = n ⟺ 10ⁿ = x to explain.' Prompt 2 — 'The M-Pesa analyst wrote log₁₀(17,000,000) ≈ 7.2304. If she makes an error and writes 7.2340 instead, will her recovered number be larger or smaller than 17,000,000? Explain without doing the full calculation.' Prompt 3 — 'A Kericho tea estate manager wants to multiply 3,240 × 47.6 using logarithms. Write out the steps he would follow, using the results from Practice Problems A and B.' After paired comparison, three pairs present to the class. The teacher uses their explanations to formalize the antilogarithm definition and to preview the log multiplication rule (log(ab) = log a + log b) without proving it yet.
framework.teacherMoves: After issuing the prompts, say: 'Write alone first — your own words, no sharing yet. Two minutes.' [WAIT 2 minutes — circulate, read over shoulders, note strong and weak explanations.] Then: 'Compare with your partner. Where do your explanations differ? Try to agree on the best wording. Two minutes.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] Cold-call Prompt 1: 'Njeri, read your explanation for prompt 1.' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After response, press: 'Good — can anyone add what the exponent 0.2304 actually represents in terms of powers of 10?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call Prompt 2: 'Kamau, is the recovered number larger or smaller? How do you know?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After response, say: 'Everyone — thumbs up if you agree, thumbs sideways if you are not sure.' Scan the room. If more than four thumbs sideways, re-examine together: 'What does a larger mantissa mean for the antilog value? Look at your antilog table — as the mantissa row number increases, do the antilog values increase or decrease?' Cold-call Prompt 3: 'Auma, walk us through the tea manager's steps.' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After she gives the steps, write on the board: log(3240) + log(47.6) = 3.7669 + 1.6776 = 5.4445 → antilog(5.4445) = ? Say: 'We have the addition step. What does taking the antilog of that sum give us? We will prove WHY addition works in Lesson 6 — but today you have just USED the procedure. Notice: the Kericho farmer's colleague did exactly this two steps.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Explanation-Driven Consolidation with Structured Prompts — The three prompts are designed at increasing levels of depth: Prompt 1 demands definitional recall; Prompt 2 demands directional reasoning without calculation (building conceptual rather than procedural knowledge); Prompt 3 demands procedural synthesis across two lessons. The public presentation of responses creates a 'talk move' environment where students hear multiple formulations of the same idea, strengthening the mental model. The teacher's deliberate withholding of the proof of log(ab) = log a + log b creates a forward tension that motivates Lesson 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads written responses during the individual writing phase. Look for: (a) students who confuse 'antilog' with 'negative log' — this is a critical misconception; address it immediately by writing antilog(0.2304) = 10^0.2304 on the board; (b) students whose Prompt 3 answer reverses the steps (antilog first, then add) — this signals the procedure has not been internalized; use a 'step-number' prompt to reorder; (c) strong responses to Prompt 2 that include reasoning such as 'the antilog table values always increase as mantissa increases' — affirm these publicly as they demonstrate table-structure understanding beyond procedural recall.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher displays the class Driving Question Board (a large chart or projected slide showing the unit's anchoring question and the accumulated evidence from Lessons 1–4). Students first examine three sticky notes the teacher has pre-prepared from the Predict phase predictions and confirm or revise them: 'Can we go from a logarithm back to the original number? YES/NO/PARTIALLY.' Students then contribute two new DQB entries per pair: (1) one 'We now know…' statement capturing today's learning; (2) one 'We still wonder…' question about something today raised but did not resolve. Selected entries are read aloud and physically added to the board. The teacher explicitly connects today's evidence to the anchoring phenomenon: 'The Kericho farmer's colleague used exactly this two-way journey — log table then antilog table — to get the answer in under two minutes. We have just done that ourselves.'
framework.teacherMoves: Bring out or project the DQB. Point to the three Predict-phase predictions recorded at lesson start. Say: 'Let's check our predictions. Achieng predicted [read it]. Mutua predicted [read it]. Wanjiru predicted [read it]. Which of these turned out to be most accurate?' [WAIT 10 seconds — accept hands.] Then say: 'On your sticky notes — one green for WE NOW KNOW, one yellow for WE STILL WONDER. You have 90 seconds. Write one statement each.' [WAIT 90 seconds.] Ask 4 pairs to read their green notes. After each, ask the class: 'Does everyone agree this belongs on our KNOW side?' Then ask 2 pairs to read yellow notes. Typical 'still wonder' entries might include: 'Why does log(ab) = log a + log b?' and 'Does this work for division too?' Say: 'Those yellow questions are exactly where Lesson 6 takes us. Notice — we have not yet proved the addition rule; we have only used it. The proof is our next evidence step.' Point to the driving question on the board and say: 'Where are we now on answering — how can the Kericho farmer use logarithms to multiply huge numbers? Can someone give me a one-sentence answer to that right now?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 1 student.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Update with Prediction Accountability — By returning to recorded predictions made at lesson start, the DQB update makes the prediction-observation-explanation cycle visible and explicit. The two-colour sticky-note protocol (green = know, yellow = wonder) distinguishes consolidated knowledge from open inquiry, preventing premature closure. The teacher's deliberate pointing to unresolved questions ('still wonder') models scientific and mathematical practice: knowing what you do not yet know is a form of understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all green and yellow notes as pairs write them. Look for: (a) green notes that are procedural only ('we know how to read the antilog table') vs. conceptual ('we know the antilog table is a table of powers of 10') — if most are procedural only, pose one more conceptual question before closing the DQB phase; (b) yellow notes that reveal residual misconceptions ('we wonder if the antilog of a negative number is a negative number') — flag these for opening of Lesson 6; (c) whether any pair can formulate a one-sentence answer to the driving question that includes both 'log table' and 'antilog table' — this demonstrates readiness for the formal log laws in Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Students retrieve their cumulative unit model — a diagram they have been building since Lesson 1 that represents the relationship between numbers, indices, and logarithms. They add three new elements to the model: (1) a two-way arrow between 'NUMBER (N)' and 'LOGARITHM (log₁₀ N)' labelled 'log table →' and '← antilog table'; (2) a box showing the four-step antilog procedure (characteristic | mantissa row | column + difference | place decimal point); (3) the M-Pesa example: 17,000,000 ↔ log₁₀(17,000,000) = 7.2304, annotated with characteristic = 7, mantissa = .2304. Students then write one sentence connecting the model to the anchoring phenomenon, beginning with the stem: 'The Kericho tea farmer's colleague was able to multiply large harvest numbers quickly because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your unit model from Lesson 1. Today we add the return journey.' Project a partially completed model on the board showing the one-way arrow from Lesson 4 (number → log). Say: 'Your job is to make this arrow two-way, and add the three elements I am about to list.' Read the three elements slowly, giving students time to draw each one. [WAIT 15 seconds after each element.] After students add the three elements (approximately 4 minutes), say: 'Now write your one sentence connecting the model to the Kericho phenomenon. Start with the stem on the board.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] Cold-call 2 students to read their sentences. After each, ask: 'Does that sentence tell us HOW as well as WHY? If not, what one word or phrase would make it more complete?' Finally, say: 'In Lesson 6 we will add one more element to this model — the log laws that prove WHY we can add logarithms instead of multiplying. Your model will be complete by Lesson 7.' Hold up a model from a previous lesson cohort (if available) to show what the completed version will look like.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision — The progressive model-building approach makes conceptual growth visible over the arc of the unit. Each revision is additive (students never erase previous entries), so the model itself becomes a learning record. The two-way arrow is the key conceptual addition in this lesson: it externalises the inverse relationship between log and antilog, which is the mathematical heart of today's learning. The sentence-stem prompt ('The Kericho tea farmer's colleague was able to…') keeps every model revision anchored to the unit phenomenon, preventing the model from becoming an abstract diagram disconnected from the motivating context.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during model revision and checks for: (a) students who draw the two arrows but label them identically — prompt: 'What is the name of the TABLE you use to go in each direction?'; (b) students whose four-step box omits the characteristic-to-decimal-point step — this is the most common procedural gap; point to their Practice Problem D answer and ask 'How did you know where to put the decimal point?'; (c) the quality of the phenomenon-connection sentence — a strong sentence names both log tables and antilog tables and references the addition of logarithms. Collect 5 models at random to assess the quality of the two-way arrow and annotation before Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Observe phase demonstration, did all learners track the table-reading procedure step by step, or did some lose the thread when I moved between the log table and the antilog table? What visual or physical cue could I add to make the switch between the two tables more salient next time?
2. When I cold-called on Prompt 2 (the M-Pesa error question), did students reason directionally (larger mantissa → larger antilog) or did they attempt a full calculation? If most attempted a full calculation, how can I design a Predict prompt in Lesson 6 that specifically rewards directional reasoning?
3. Were the four skeleton-sheet practice problems correctly calibrated — too easy (all pairs finished in under 5 minutes), about right (most pairs finished with 1–2 minutes to spare), or too hard (more than a quarter of pairs did not reach Problem D)? Adjust the number and difficulty of practice problems accordingly.
4. Looking at the 5 unit models I collected: do students show the antilog as the inverse of the log, or do they show it as a separate unrelated process? If models show it as separate, I need to open Lesson 6 with an explicit 'these two arrows are inverses of each other — just as multiplication and division are inverses' bridge.
5. Did the M-Pesa context feel genuinely motivating to students, or did it feel like a forced application? Observe whether students spontaneously use M-Pesa or other Kenyan financial contexts in their 'We Now Know / We Still Wonder' sticky notes as an indicator of authentic engagement with the phenomenon.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Students observed a teacher-modelled, narrated demonstration of the full four-step antilogarithm table procedure, applied to the M-Pesa transaction volume of 17,000,000 (log₁₀ = 7.2304). They also observed that pressing the 10ˣ key on a scientific calculator gives the same result as the antilog table, confirming that both tools are performing the same mathematical operation — raising 10 to a power.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The antilogarithm of x is 10ˣ; finding it requires separating the characteristic from the mantissa, looking up the mantissa in the antilog table (row = first two decimal digits, column = third decimal digit, mean-difference = fourth decimal digit), and using the characteristic to place the decimal point in the result. Together with the log table procedure from Lesson 4, students can now make the full two-way journey between any number and its common logarithm.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The anchoring phenomenon — how the Kericho farmer's colleague multiplied two large harvest numbers in under two minutes using only a table — can now be traced step by step: (1) find log of each number using the log table; (2) add the two logarithms (a step students have used but not yet proved); (3) find the antilog of the sum using the antilog table to recover the product. Today's lesson provides step 3, completing the procedure. The proof that step 2 is valid (log(ab) = log a + log b) is the open question that motivates Lesson 6.

LESSONS.title: Applying Logarithms to Multiplication and Division

slo.purpose: Learners apply the logarithm laws log(ab) = log a + log b and log(a/b) = log a − log b to perform multi-digit multiplication and division using four-figure mathematical tables, replicating the 'farmer's two-minute calculation' from the anchoring phenomenon and solving real-life Kenyan problems involving bulk maize pricing, fertiliser mixing ratios, and export tonnage.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) state and explain the product law of logarithms: log(ab) = log a + log b; (b) state and explain the quotient law of logarithms: log(a/b) = log a − log b; (c) use four-figure logarithm tables to find the logarithm and antilogarithm of numbers; (d) apply both laws to evaluate products and quotients of multi-digit numbers.
slo.skills: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) read logarithm and antilogarithm tables accurately, including the use of the difference columns; (b) set up a standard logarithm working table (number | log | operation | result); (c) perform multi-step multiplication and division computations using logarithms within two minutes per problem; (d) verify reasonableness of answers using estimation.
slo.attitudes: The learner: (a) appreciates that converting multiplication into addition is an elegant mathematical idea that empowered farmers and scientists before calculators existed; (b) shows patience and precision when reading four-figure tables; (c) values collaborative problem-solving when working with a partner on real-life Kenyan contexts.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use logarithms in computations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is Lesson 6 of 8 in the evidence-gathering sequence. In Lessons 1–5 learners built index notation, established log as the inverse of a power, and read basic log tables. Now they execute the full 'farmer's two-minute calculation' that was promised in the anchoring phenomenon — multiplying and dividing large numbers by adding and subtracting their logarithms. By the end of this lesson learners can replicate the technical-training demonstration the fellow Kericho farmer performed, directly answering the driving question's challenge of handling numbers too large for ordinary arithmetic.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials are used. Ensure printed four-figure log tables are handled carefully and not written on (shared class sets). If digital devices are used to display tables, apply screen-time guidelines as per school policy.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by re-examining the side-by-side comparison from the anchoring phenomenon (long multiplication vs. logarithm method) and predict which law makes multiplication possible with logarithms. Through guided pair-work they derive the product and quotient laws, then practise reading antilogarithm tables. The core activity has pairs solving three real-life Kenyan problems — bulk maize pricing at Wakulima Market, fertiliser mixing ratios for a Rift Valley farm, and export tonnage from Mombasa port — using a structured log working table. A class gallery share consolidates the method, and learners update their Driving Question Board and cumulative model before a teacher-led exit reflection ties every step back to the Kericho tea farmer phenomenon.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown the two side-by-side worked examples from the anchoring phenomenon displayed on a poster or board: (A) long multiplication of 2¹⁰ × 8 = 1024 × 8 done digit-by-digit, and (B) the same calculation done in two lines using log tables. Each learner independently writes in their exercise book: (1) Which step in Method B replaces the multiplication sign — and what arithmetic operation does it use instead? (2) If log(1024) ≈ 3.0103 and log(8) ≈ 0.9031, predict the answer to log(1024 × 8) before looking it up. (3) Write one sentence explaining, in your own words, why you think adding logarithms might give the same result as multiplying the original numbers. Learners share predictions with their partner for 90 seconds before the teacher takes cold-call responses.
framework.teacherMoves: Post the two side-by-side worked examples on the board before learners enter. Once settled, say: 'Look carefully at these two calculations — both find the same answer. In your book, answer the three questions on the board. You have 4 minutes working silently.' [Allow 4 minutes independent think time.] After 4 minutes: 'Share your prediction for question 2 with your partner. You have 90 seconds.' [Allow 90 seconds.] Cold-call 3 pairs: 'Amina and Odhiambo — what operation did you identify in question 1?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] 'Fatuma and Kipkoech — what number did you predict for log(1024 × 8)?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] 'Wanjiku and Mwangi — read us your one-sentence explanation for question 3.' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Record all three predicted answers on the board without evaluating correctness. Say: 'We will test every one of these predictions today. Keep them visible — you will come back to them.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-Test (Anchored Prediction): Learners commit to a specific numeric prediction (log(1024 × 8) ≈ 3.9134) before instruction, creating cognitive dissonance that will be resolved when the law is derived. Connecting the prediction to the phenomenon's side-by-side comparison ensures the lesson opens inside the storyline rather than as an abstract rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has written a numeric prediction and a sentence in their book before the cold-call. Teacher scans books during the 90-second partner share. Red flag: If fewer than half the class attempt question 2, pause and re-display the two logarithm values on the board. Note which students predicted 'addition' vs. other operations — this reveals whether prior log-as-inverse knowledge from Lesson 5 is secure.

framework.learnerExperience: PART A — Deriving the Laws (20 min). Each pair receives a structured discovery worksheet. Step 1: Using index laws already known, learners complete: 10^a × 10^b = 10^(a+b). Step 2: If log(M) = a and log(N) = b, then M = 10^a and N = 10^b. Write M × N in terms of powers of 10. Step 3: Apply log to both sides of M × N = 10^(a+b). What do you get? Step 4: Replace a with log M and b with log N to state the product law. Step 5: Repeat for M ÷ N to derive the quotient law. Pairs write both laws in a coloured box in their books. PART B — Reading Antilogarithm Tables (10 min). Teacher models live on the board: 'To find antilog(3.9134), I look up 3.9134 in the antilog table. The characteristic 3 tells me the answer is in the thousands. The mantissa .9134 — I find row .91, column 3, difference column 4. I read 8190. So antilog(3.9134) = 8190.' Learners immediately practise three guided lookups: antilog(2.7482), antilog(0.4771), antilog(1.3010). They write each result and check with the pair.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the discovery worksheets. Say: 'Work through Steps 1 to 5 with your partner. You already know index laws from Lesson 2 — this is you discovering where the log law comes from. You have 10 minutes.' [Circulate. After 5 minutes, pause the class.] Cold-call one pair to write Step 3 on the board: 'Njeri and Barasa — come and write what you got at Step 3.' [WAIT 10 seconds for them to approach.] Correct any errors immediately, reinforcing: 'log(M × N) = log(10^(a+b)) = a + b = log M + log N — this is the product law.' Repeat for quotient law with a second pair. Then say: 'Box both laws in colour — these are the tools the Kericho farmer used.' For Part B, say: 'Watch me read the antilog table carefully — I will do it slowly.' Model step-by-step as described. Then: 'Now you try the three lookups. I will cold-call in 5 minutes.' [WAIT 5 minutes.] Cold-call 3 different pairs for the three lookups, asking: 'Kipchoge and Akinyi — what is antilog(2.7482) and how did you read the table?' [WAIT 12 seconds each time.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Guided Algebraic Derivation (Structured Discovery): Rather than stating the laws, learners re-derive them from known index laws using a scaffolded worksheet. This strategy makes the 'magic' of the phenomenon explicable — the product law is not mysterious once learners see it follows directly from 10^a × 10^b = 10^(a+b). Connecting each algebraic step back to 'M = amount of tea produced, N = number of plants' keeps the phenomenon alive during derivation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: At Step 3 of the worksheet, every learner should write 'log(M × N) = a + b'. Teacher checks this specific line during circulation — it is the pivotal deduction. Red flag: Students who write 'log(M) × log(N) = a + b' are confusing multiplication of logs with the log of a product; address immediately with: 'Careful — log is applied to the whole product M × N, not to log M times log N.' For antilog practice: correct reading is antilog(2.7482) = 560.0, antilog(0.4771) = 3.000, antilog(1.3010) = 20.00. Students getting the order of magnitude wrong (forgetting the characteristic) are identified here.

framework.learnerExperience: Pairs solve three real-life problems using a standard four-row log working table (Number | Logarithm | Operation | Result). All problems are set in Kenyan contexts: PROBLEM 1 (Multiplication): A maize trader at Wakulima Market, Nairobi, buys 346 bags each weighing 91.5 kg. Using logarithms, find the total mass of maize purchased. PROBLEM 2 (Division): A fertiliser depot in Nakuru has 7,820 kg of CAN fertiliser to distribute equally among 34 farms in the Rift Valley. Using logarithms, find the mass each farm receives. PROBLEM 3 (Combined): A tea estate in Kericho produces 2,480 kg of processed tea per week. The estate operates for 52 weeks per year. The Kenya Tea Development Agency (KTDA) buys the tea at Ksh 118 per kg. Using logarithms, calculate the annual revenue. (This requires multiplication twice or a combined log calculation.) Each pair records full working in their books. After completing all three, pairs write a one-sentence 'connection statement': 'This method works because ________, which is exactly what the fellow Kericho farmer showed in the two-minute calculation.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now you are the technical-training farmers. You will solve three real Kenyan problems the same way the fellow farmer did — using logarithms instead of a calculator. Work in your pairs. You have 18 minutes.' [Distribute printed log and antilog table booklets if not already in use. Write the three problems on the board.] Circulate actively. After 6 minutes (when most should finish Problem 1), pause: 'Hands up if you have the answer to Problem 1.' [Scan.] 'Opiyo and Chebet — read your log working table for Problem 1 row by row.' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Correct any table-reading errors on the board live. After 12 minutes, briefly address Problem 2 in the same way. After 18 minutes, cold-call one pair per problem to present full working on the board: 'Zawadi and Mutua — write your complete working for Problem 3 on the board. Talk us through each row of your table.' [WAIT 15 seconds.] After each presentation, ask the class: 'Thumbs up if your answer matches, thumbs sideways if slightly different, thumbs down if very different.' Address discrepancies. Finally, ask all pairs to write their connection statement and cold-call two: 'Read your connection statement.' [WAIT 12 seconds each.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Log Working Table (Procedural Scaffolding with Contextual Meaning): The four-column table (Number | Logarithm | Operation | Result) makes the invisible steps of the method visible and auditable. Pairing this scaffold with Kenya-specific contexts (Wakulima Market, KTDA, Nakuru depots) ensures learners experience the method as genuinely useful rather than abstract. The 'connection statement' forces explicit linguistic linking back to the phenomenon, consolidating sensemaking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Problem 1 expected answer: log(346) + log(91.5) = 2.5391 + 1.9614 = 4.5005; antilog(4.5005) ≈ 31,640 kg — correct order of magnitude is critical. (2) Problem 2: log(7820) − log(34) = 3.8932 − 1.5315 = 2.3617; antilog(2.3617) ≈ 229.9 kg per farm. (3) Problem 3: log(2480) + log(52) + log(118) = 3.3945 + 1.7160 + 2.0719 = 7.1824; antilog(7.1824) ≈ 15,220,000 Ksh annually. Red flag for Problem 3: Students who add only two logs have missed that revenue = production × weeks × price; prompt with: 'How many numbers are being multiplied together? How many logs should you add?' Students confusing characteristic and mantissa during antilog lookup need one-to-one table coaching during circulation.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes two sticky notes (or index-card strips if physical DQB is used): GREEN NOTE — one thing they can now explain about the driving question: 'How can a Kericho tea farmer use logarithms to calculate with very large numbers?' Specifically, they must use the words 'product law' or 'quotient law' in their green note. ORANGE NOTE — one remaining question or uncertainty, for example: 'Can logarithms also handle powers and roots?' or 'What happens when we multiply three or more numbers?' or 'Why does the antilog table have a differences column?' Learners post their notes on the class DQB under the columns 'We Now Understand' and 'We Still Wonder'. The teacher reads 3–4 orange notes aloud to the class and previews: 'Lesson 7 will answer the question about powers and roots — stay curious.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two minutes to write your two notes — green must include the words product law or quotient law. Orange can be anything you still genuinely wonder about.' [Allow 2 minutes.] As learners post notes, circulate and read them. Select 3 green notes that show strong connection to the phenomenon and read them aloud: 'Listen to how Amara connected this to the Kericho farmer...' Then read 3 orange notes and say: 'These are excellent scientific questions. Notice that Kibet is asking about powers — that is exactly where we are going next lesson.' Point to the DQB and say: 'Look at how much of the board has moved from the Wonder side to the Understand side since Lesson 1. The farmer's two-minute calculation is no longer mysterious to you.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Update (Metacognitive Tracking): The DQB serves as a visible record of the class's growing understanding across all 8 lessons. Requiring the specific terms 'product law' or 'quotient law' in the green note ensures disciplinary vocabulary is consolidated. The orange notes surface genuine curiosity about powers and roots, which is the content of Lesson 7, creating a learner-generated bridge between lessons and maintaining storyline momentum.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every green note correctly names either the product or quotient law and connects it to a computation context (maize, fertiliser, tea). Red flag: Green notes that say only 'I learned log(ab) = log a + log b' without any contextual connection indicate surface-level recall rather than sensemaking — pull these students aside for a brief verbal probe: 'How would the Kericho farmer actually use this law? Walk me through one step.' Orange notes asking about negative logarithms or logarithms of numbers less than 1 indicate high readiness and should be noted for extension in Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner opens their cumulative model page — a diagram begun in Lesson 1 that represents how the Kericho tea farmer's calculation works. In earlier lessons, learners added: index notation for repeated multiplication (Lesson 1–2), the definition of logarithm as the inverse operation (Lesson 3–4), and the method for reading log tables (Lesson 5). Today, learners add two new components: (A) A labelled arrow from 'MULTIPLY two quantities' pointing to 'CONVERT each to its logarithm (look up in table)' → 'ADD the logarithms' → 'CONVERT answer back using antilog table' → 'FINAL PRODUCT'. (B) A parallel arrow for DIVISION showing subtraction of logarithms. Below the diagram, learners write a two-sentence summary: 'The product law works because multiplying powers of 10 means adding their exponents, which is what logarithms are. This is why the Kericho farmer can find the total tea revenue — Ksh 15,220,000 — by adding three small decimal numbers from a table instead of multiplying three large numbers together.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative model page. You are adding the most powerful piece yet — the full calculation chain that the fellow farmer demonstrated. Draw the two arrows I describe and label every box.' [Allow 5 minutes for drawing and labelling.] Circulate and check that both the multiplication chain and the division chain are present. After 5 minutes: 'Write your two-sentence summary underneath the diagram. First sentence: why the law works. Second sentence: connect it to the Kericho farmer with a specific number from today.' [Allow 3 minutes.] Cold-call two learners to read their two-sentence summaries: 'Miriam — read your summary.' [WAIT 12 seconds.] 'Otieno — read yours.' [WAIT 12 seconds.] After both, say: 'Notice Miriam connected back to index laws from Lesson 2 — that is exactly the chain of reasoning we have been building for six lessons. In Lesson 7, this model will grow again when we tackle powers and roots.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Visual Model Revision (Progressive Model Building): The diagram grows across all 8 lessons, making the unit's conceptual arc visible to every learner at a glance. Adding today's calculation chain directly onto a model that already contains index notation and log-as-inverse reinforces the coherence of the entire unit. Requiring a specific number (Ksh 15,220,000) in the summary sentence anchors the abstract model to the concrete phenomenon and discourages generic statements.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: The completed model addition shows a correctly sequenced four-box chain (multiply → log → add → antilog) for multiplication, and a matching chain for division (divide → log → subtract → antilog). The two-sentence summary explicitly names index laws as the reason the product law works. Red flag: Models that show only the addition step without the antilog step are incomplete — the 'converting back' step is frequently omitted and represents a procedural gap that will cause errors in Lesson 7 when powers are involved. Red flag sentence: 'The law works because logs are easier' — this is vague; prompt with 'What specific property of powers of 10 makes this work?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) PHENOMENON CONNECTION — In the Explain phase, did learners spontaneously refer back to the Kericho farmer when discussing their solutions, or did the Kenyan contexts feel like add-ons rather than genuine motivators? If the latter, consider opening Lesson 7 by re-reading the original phenomenon statement aloud and asking: 'Which part of that story can you now fully explain?' (2) TABLE-READING ACCURACY — Were errors concentrated in reading the log table (finding the mantissa) or in the antilog table (applying the differences column), or in assigning the characteristic? Identifying the specific failure point allows you to provide a targeted 5-minute micro-revision at the start of Lesson 7. (3) PARTNER DYNAMICS — Did both members of each pair engage with the log working table, or did one partner dominate while the other copied? Consider assigning roles in Lesson 7: 'Table Reader' (reads the log value aloud) and 'Recorder' (writes the working table row), alternating per problem. (4) PROBLEM 3 CHALLENGE — The three-factor multiplication in Problem 3 (production × weeks × price) was the highest cognitive demand of the lesson. Note which pairs solved it correctly and which added only two logs. Use correct pairs as peer-tutors in the opening minutes of Lesson 7 before extending to powers and roots. (5) DQB QUALITY — Were the orange 'wonder' notes genuinely curious about powers and roots, or were they expressing confusion about today's content? If more than one-third express confusion about the basic product law, build a brief consolidation activity into the first 10 minutes of Lesson 7 before advancing the storyline.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed two side-by-side worked examples — long multiplication of large tea-harvest numbers versus the same calculation performed using four-figure logarithm tables — and noted that the logarithm method replaced a multiplication step with an addition step, producing the same result in a fraction of the time.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners derived the product law log(ab) = log a + log b and the quotient law log(a/b) = log a − log b directly from the index law 10^a × 10^b = 10^(a+b), and applied both laws using four-figure log and antilog tables to solve real-life Kenyan problems involving bulk maize pricing at Wakulima Market, fertiliser distribution in the Rift Valley, and annual tea revenue for a Kericho KTDA estate.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The reason multiplying two numbers is equivalent to adding their logarithms is that logarithms are exponents of powers of 10, and multiplying powers of 10 means adding their exponents — so log(M × N) = log M + log N follows directly from the index law. This is exactly the mathematical principle that allowed the fellow Kericho farmer to complete the tea-harvest revenue calculation in under two minutes using only a log table, converting an unwieldy multi-digit multiplication into a simple decimal addition.
